title: 🌍 Civic Sense Champion
theme: Lead community improvement and become an active citizen
description: Your neighborhood needs a champion! With 500 Mento Coins and passion for change, lead community improvement initiatives. Tackle littering, traffic safety, park renovation, or digital divide. Engage stakeholders, build coalitions, navigate local politics, and create lasting positive impact. Will you be the civic leader your community needs?

how_to_play.title: How to Play
steps: Read each community scenario and understand the civic challenge presented
Choose from the available options -- each choice affects your resources and community metrics
Manage your Campaign Budget, Community Support, and Government Relations wisely
Build volunteer teams and complete community projects across multiple rounds
Aim to maximize your Civic Awareness and Projects Completed by the final round
tips: Balance community support and government approval -- you need both to succeed
Investing in volunteers early pays off in later rounds with more project capacity
Media coverage can boost your cause but may also attract unwanted scrutiny

learning_objectives: Understand the role of active citizenship in identifying and solving local community problems such as waste management, traffic safety, and digital inclusion
Develop coalition-building skills by engaging diverse stakeholders including government officials, business owners, and grassroots activists
Practice democratic participation through public speaking, petition drives, town hall presentations, and policy advocacy
Learn to navigate opposition and conflict constructively using dialogue, compromise, transparency, and evidence-based persuasion
Explore strategies for scaling civic impact beyond a single neighborhood through replication, policy change, and leadership mentoring

rounds.title: Round 1: Choose Your Community Challenge
rounds.story:
Welcome to civic engagement!

Your neighborhood has several problems that need solutions. You have {{mento_coins}} Mento Coins, {{volunteer_count}} volunteers, and unlimited passion.

But you can only focus on ONE issue effectively. Which community problem will you tackle?

Research shows successful civic initiatives:
• Focus on specific, solvable problems
• Build coalitions across different groups
• Create visible, measurable impact
• Sustain momentum over time

Your choice will determine your approach, stakeholders, and impact metrics.
rounds.goal: Identify the community problem you'll solve

choices.label: Littering & Waste Management
choices.description: Streets and parks filled with trash. No recycling program. People don't know proper disposal. Start cleanup drives, recycling education, install bins. Visible impact, easy to measure.
choices.feedback: Waste management chosen! Practical, visible problem with immediate impact. You'll organize cleanup drives, educate on recycling, and work with city on permanent solutions.

choices.label: Traffic Safety Near School
choices.description: Dangerous crossing near school. Kids nearly hit by cars. No crosswalk, lights, or speed bumps. Need to convince city to install safety measures. Requires government engagement.
choices.feedback: Traffic safety chosen! Child safety is compelling issue. You'll need petition drives, city council presentations, and sustained advocacy to get infrastructure changes approved.

choices.label: Abandoned Park Renovation
choices.description: Beautiful park now neglected - broken equipment, overgrown plants, unsafe. Restore as community gathering space. Requires funding, volunteers, and city partnership.
choices.feedback: Park renovation chosen! Community spaces bring people together. Large visible project requiring sustained effort, diverse skills, and broad coalition building.

choices.label: Digital Divide - Tech Access for Elderly
choices.description: Elderly neighbors isolated, can't use smartphones/internet. Can't access services, connect with family, or participate in digital world. Tech education program needed.
choices.feedback: Digital inclusion chosen! Addresses isolation and access to services. You'll create tech workshops for seniors, teaching internet, video calls, and online services. Intergenerational impact!

rounds.image_prompt: a vibrant neighborhood park bustling with families, children playing on swings, volunteers discussing plans at picnic tables, sunlight filtering through leafy trees, a sense of community spirit
rounds.coaching_moment: Consider how this choice affects your long-term resources, not just the immediate gain.
rounds.reflection_prompt: What tradeoff did this decision reveal? What did you gain, and what did you give up?

expert_pick.reason: The most effective leaders adapt their approach based on the situation — not habit.

rounds.title: Round 2: Build Your Coalition
rounds.story:
You've identified the problem! Now you need SUPPORT.

Current Status:
• Budget: {{mento_coins}} MC
• Community Support: {{community_support}}%
• Volunteers: {{volunteer_count}}
• Government Relations: {{government_approval}}%

Successful civic initiatives require coalition building:
• Identify stakeholders
• Understand their interests
• Find common ground
• Build lasting relationships

How will you build support for your initiative?
rounds.goal: Build coalition of supporters and stakeholders

choices.label: Grassroots Door-to-Door Campaign
choices.description: Go house-to-house talking to neighbors. Time-intensive but builds authentic relationships and trust. People appreciate face-to-face conversation.
choices.feedback: Door-to-door campaign! Old-school but effective. You spend weekends knocking on doors, listening to concerns, building relationships. People appreciate being heard. Slow but solid foundation.

choices.label: Social Media Awareness Campaign
choices.description: Create compelling content, viral videos, online petition. Reach hundreds quickly but less personal. Good for awareness, harder for deep engagement.
choices.feedback: Social media campaign launched! Your videos go viral locally. Hundreds of likes, shares, and signups. Fast reach but you'll need to convert online support into real-world action.

choices.label: Partner with Existing Organizations
choices.description: Approach established community groups - church, rotary club, PTA, local businesses. Leverage their networks and credibility. Faster but need to align with their missions.
choices.feedback: Strategic partnerships formed! You present at Rotary Club, partner with PTA, get church to announce. Leveraging established trust and networks. Professional approach that opens doors.

choices.label: Direct Government Engagement
choices.description: Start with officials - mayor, council members, city departments. Get official support first, then use it to build community buy-in. Top-down approach but can be effective.
choices.feedback: Government-first strategy! You schedule meetings with councilwoman, present to planning department, meet mayor. Official support secured, but some community members feel left out of process.

rounds.image_prompt: a vibrant community center bustling with diverse groups of people engaging in discussions, colorful posters on the walls promoting unity, sunlight streaming through large windows
rounds.coaching_moment: Think about trade-offs: what are you giving up to get this benefit?

expert_pick.reason: Calculated risk-taking is what separates growth-oriented leaders from status-quo managers.

rounds.title: Round 3: Execute Your Project
rounds.story:
Coalition built! Time for ACTION.

Current Status:
• Budget: {{mento_coins}} MC
• Community Support: {{community_support}}%
• Volunteers: {{volunteer_count}} ready to work!
• Government Approval: {{government_approval}}%
• Media Coverage: {{media_coverage}}%

Now the hard work begins. Theory becomes practice. Plans become reality.

How will you implement your initiative?
rounds.goal: Successfully execute your community improvement project

choices.label: Small Pilot Program First
choices.description: Start small in one area, learn lessons, then scale. Reduces risk, allows course correction. Takes longer but more sustainable.
choices.feedback: Pilot approach! You test in one neighborhood first. Discover what works, what doesn't. Build proof of concept before scaling. Smart, evidence-based approach to social change.

choices.label: Big Community Launch Event
choices.description: Organize major kickoff event - speeches, media, celebration. Generate excitement and momentum. High visibility but all eggs in one basket.
choices.feedback: Major launch event! 200 people attend. Mayor speaks. Local news covers. Social media buzzes. Massive momentum but now you MUST deliver on the hype. High risk, high reward!

choices.label: Sustained Weekly Actions
choices.description: Regular weekly activities - cleanup every Saturday, meetings every Wednesday. Build habit and routine. Less flashy but builds lasting culture.
choices.feedback: Sustained action model! Every Saturday cleanup becomes neighborhood tradition. Core volunteers develop strong bonds. Less exciting than big event but creates lasting culture of engagement.

choices.label: Focus on Policy Change
choices.description: Work on getting official rules/policies changed. Petition, council presentations, public hearings. Systemic change but slower and harder.
choices.feedback: Policy change strategy! You present to city council, organize public testimony, build coalition of officials. Addressing root causes through systemic change. This is how democracies work!

rounds.image_prompt: a bustling community center filled with enthusiastic volunteers at work, colorful posters of the project on the walls, bright lights illuminating a vibrant atmosphere of teamwork and energy
rounds.coaching_moment: How might your team react to this decision? What about your customers?
rounds.reflection_prompt: Why did you choose this option? What were you trying to protect or grow?

expert_pick.reason: The most effective leaders adapt their approach based on the situation — not habit.

rounds.title: Round 4: Handling Opposition & Setbacks
rounds.story:
Not everyone supports your initiative!

Current Status:
• Community Support: {{community_support}}%
• Government Approval: {{government_approval}}%
• Projects: {{projects_completed}} completed

CRISIS: A group of residents opposes your project:
• 'It costs too much!'
• 'Change is disruptive!'
• 'Youth don't understand!'
• Starting petition against you

This is normal in civic engagement. How you respond matters more than the opposition itself.

How will you handle this constructively?
rounds.goal: Navigate opposition while maintaining community support

choices.label: Ignore and Push Forward
choices.description: Stay focused on supporters, don't engage critics. They're minority. Keep working. Risk: Division deepens, they organize stronger opposition.
choices.feedback: You push forward despite opposition. Project continues but community is now divided. Opposition grows stronger. You accomplished goals but at cost of community unity. Sometimes winning creates losers.

choices.label: Host Community Dialogue Session
choices.description: Invite opposition to public dialogue. Listen to concerns, find common ground, adjust plans if needed. Takes time but builds consensus. Democratic process.
choices.feedback: Community dialogue hosted! You listen for 2 hours to concerns. Some valid points about costs. You adjust plan to address their concerns. They're not enemies - just neighbors with different views. This is democracy!

choices.label: Propose Compromise Solution
choices.description: Modify your plan to address their concerns. Scale back costs, phased approach, more community input. Neither side gets everything but both get something.
choices.feedback: Compromise proposed! You create modified plan incorporating their cost concerns. Not your original vision but brings community together. Politics is the art of the possible.

choices.label: Full Transparency Campaign
choices.description: Address concerns head-on with data, budget breakdowns, testimonials. Educate community on why project matters. Fact-based persuasion.
choices.feedback: Transparency campaign! You publish detailed budgets, impact data, testimonials from beneficiaries. Respond to every concern with facts and evidence. Some opposition softens when they see the data.

rounds.image_prompt: a vibrant town square filled with concerned residents, some holding protest signs, while a few engage in calm discussions, colorful banners fluttering in the breeze, sunlight filtering through trees
rounds.coaching_moment: Look at your current resource levels — which constraint are you trying to address?

expert_pick.reason: The most effective leaders adapt their approach based on the situation — not habit.

rounds.title: Round 5: Scaling Your Impact
rounds.story:
Success! Your initiative is working!

Results:
• Community Support: {{community_support}}%
• Projects Completed: {{projects_completed}}
• Volunteers: {{volunteer_count}}
• Media Coverage: {{media_coverage}}%

Other neighborhoods notice. State government pays attention. You've proven the model works.

Now the question: How do you scale impact beyond your immediate community?
rounds.goal: Scale your civic initiative for broader impact

choices.label: Replicate in Other Neighborhoods
choices.description: Help other communities start similar initiatives. Create toolkit, train new leaders. Multiplicative impact but less control.
choices.feedback: Replication strategy! You create 'How To' guide and train 5 other youth leaders. Your model spreading across city. You're building a movement, not just a project!

choices.label: Push for City-Wide Policy
choices.description: Work with government to make your solution official city policy. Systemic change at scale. Requires political skill and patience.
choices.feedback: Policy advocacy! You campaign for city council to adopt your approach city-wide. After 6 months, they pass resolution! Your community initiative is now official policy. This is systemic change!

choices.label: Form Non-Profit Organization
choices.description: Establish formal 501(c)(3) organization. Hire staff, raise funds, professionalize. Sustainable but bureaucratic.
choices.feedback: Non-profit formed! You file paperwork, recruit board of directors, apply for grants. Your grassroots project is now formal organization. Can sustain beyond you but loses some spontaneity.

choices.label: Train Next Generation of Leaders
choices.description: Focus on teaching others your skills. Youth leadership academy. Impact through capacity building. Legacy approach.
choices.feedback: Youth leadership academy launched! You train 30 middle schoolers in civic engagement. They start their own projects. You're not just solving problems - you're creating problem-solvers. This is legacy!

rounds.image_prompt: a vibrant community gathering in a park, people celebrating with colorful banners and balloons, children playing, volunteers discussing plans at a picnic table under bright sunshine
rounds.coaching_moment: Sometimes the bold choice carries risk, but also the highest reward. Weigh carefully.
rounds.reflection_prompt: If this were a real business decision, what extra information would you want?

expert_pick.reason: Resilience research shows that processing setbacks openly builds stronger teams.

glossary_terms.definition: Active participation in the life of a community to improve conditions for others or shape the community's future. Includes voting, volunteering, attending meetings, and advocacy.
glossary_terms.example: Organizing neighborhood cleanup, attending town hall, starting petition for safer crosswalks - all forms of civic engagement.

glossary_terms.definition: Bringing together diverse groups and individuals to work toward common goal. Essential for social change because most issues require broad support.
glossary_terms.example: To fix park, you build coalition of parents (safety), seniors (benches), youth (sports), and businesses (funding).

glossary_terms.definition: Building power from the ground up through individual relationships and community mobilization. Bottom-up rather than top-down approach to change.
glossary_terms.example: Door-to-door campaigns, community meetings, volunteer networks - power built through people, not institutions.

glossary_terms.definition: Any person or group affected by or able to affect an issue. In civic work, identifying and engaging stakeholders is crucial for success.
glossary_terms.example: For traffic safety: stakeholders include students, parents, school, drivers, city officials, nearby businesses.

glossary_terms.definition: Networks of relationships among people who live and work in a society, enabling it to function effectively. Trust, norms, and connections that create community strength.
glossary_terms.example: Neighborhood where people know and help each other has high social capital. Makes collective action easier.
